Purify
PYUR-ih-fy
v.
From Latin purificare, “to make pure,” from purus (pure) + facere (to make). Renders the Greek hagnizō, “to make holy, set apart for purity,” and the Hebrew tāhēr, “to be clean,” and zāqaq, “to refine, as metal.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To purify is to make pure—to free a person or thing from defilement, so that it stands clean and fit for God. The biblical doctrine ranges across ceremonial purification (the rites of cleansing under the law), the moral purification of the heart by faith (Acts 15:9: purifying their hearts by faith), the practical purification of the believer’s life by the indwelling Spirit and the obeyed Word (1 Pet 1:22: ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren), and the eschatological self-purification of the saint who hopes to see his Lord: every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure (1 John 3:3). The verb is therefore both passive and active: the believer is purified by Christ’s blood and by the Spirit (Tit 2:14: Christ gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works); and the believer purifies himself in the daily mortification of sin and pursuit of holiness, in the strength of grace, with the hope of glory as motive. Purification is the great theme of the whole sanctifying enterprise: as the refiner sits over the silver, watching the dross come off until he can see his own face in the molten metal, so the Lord sits over His people, applying the fire of His Word, providence, and Spirit until the image of His Son is formed in them. The eschatological purification is the climax: at His coming, when we see Him as He is, we shall be like Him—the long work of purification carried to its completion in the resurrection body and the glorified soul.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PURIFY as to make pure or clear; to free from extraneous admixture; in a moral sense, to make pure; to free from guilt or the defilement of sin; in religion, to free from ceremonial uncleanness.

expand to see more

PURIFY, v.t. — 1. To make pure or clear; to free from extraneous admixture; as, to purify liquors or metals. 2. To free from anything noxious or contagious; as, to purify the air. 3. In a moral sense, to make pure; to free from guilt or the defilement of sin; to free from improper mixture of any kind; as, to purify the heart. 4. In religion, to free from ceremonial uncleanness.

PURIFICATION, n. — The act of cleansing or making pure; in religion, a cleansing from the guilt of sin; also, the act of separating from anything noxious.

📖 Key Scripture

1 John 3:3 — "And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure."

Titus 2:14 — "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works."

Acts 15:9 — "And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith."

Malachi 3:3 — "And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Purification is corrupted by the aesthetic-and-wellness register of the age, which reduces purity to skincare regimens, ‘clean’ eating, and lifestyle hygiene, while the substantive doctrine of the heart purified by faith and the soul purified by the indwelling Spirit is forgotten.

expand to see more

The age has shifted purification from the moral to the aesthetic register. Where Scripture speaks of the heart purified by faith, the soul purified in obeying the truth, and the saint who in hope of his Lord’s appearing purifies himself even as He is pure, the contemporary culture speaks of skincare purification, ‘clean’ eating, detox routines, and lifestyle hygiene. The vocabulary survives; the referent has shifted. Purity has become a category of personal aesthetic and dietary cleanliness with no inward reference, while the inward purification on which Scripture insists—the cleansing of the heart, the conscience, and the affections by the blood and Spirit of Christ—is left largely unaddressed. The result is a generation that pursues aesthetic purity with religious intensity and inward purity with cultural indifference.

Recover the biblical center, and aesthetic purity falls into its modest place while moral purity returns to its proper urgency. The body is to be cared for; cleanliness is a small good. But the heart is what God watches, and the heart can be skincare-perfect and morally filthy at once. The doctrine of purification calls the saint to the daily, Spirit-empowered work of mortifying impurity in thought, affection, speech, and behavior; to the active hope of seeing Christ, which is the great motive of self-purification in 1 John 3; and to the patient endurance of the Refiner’s fire, by which the dross of indwelling sin is gradually removed until the image of the Son can be seen in the saint as in the refiner’s silver.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hagnizō (to make holy, purify); Hebrew tāhēr (to be clean) and zāqaq (to refine, as metal)—the heart purified by faith, the soul purified by the Spirit, the saint purifying himself in hope of his Lord.

expand to see more

Greek hagnizō (G48) — to make pure, purify; the verb of 1 John 3:3 and Acts 21:24.

Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, chaste, holy (the adjective).

Hebrew tāhēr (H2891) — to be clean, pure—the major ceremonial-purity verb.

Hebrew zāqaq (H2212) — to refine, distill, purify (as gold or silver).

Usage

"Every man that has this hope in him purifies himself, even as He is pure—the saint’s active self-purification is hope-driven."

"The heart is purified by faith and the soul by the Spirit; aesthetic cleanliness reaches neither."

"Christ purified to Himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works—purification is part of redemption, not a separate program."
